text: Five storeys of grey plaster, falling off in slabs to show the brick underneath. Every window has a curtain, and behind every curtain, somebody is watching the man with the goose.
Somebody's washing, frozen solid. That shirt could stand up and walk to work by itself.
Brown-coal briquettes. The whole of East Berlin smells of them in winter: sulphur, smoke and faint despair.
Every briquette in this pile is counted. Probably by two different ministries.
The door to Ilse's stairwell. Her flat is on the fourth floor, with a view of the bins and a microphone in the light fitting.
Not upstairs, Jack. The neighbour on the second floor writes down everyone who uses the stairs. She has written down me forty times.
The Trabant, running, and smoking like a steam engine. A fishnet fan belt. Somewhere in Zwickau an engineer is weeping.
A Trabant 601: a two-stroke engine, a body made of cotton waste and resin, and a waiting list of twelve years. Its bonnet is up and Uwe's head is in it.
Get in? And go where? Without a fan belt it goes nowhere. It does not even go "brrm".
The archway out to the street. A Volkspolizei van has been parked across the road for an hour. Nobody has got in or out of it.
Ilse, in her red coat, the only bright colour in Prenzlauer Berg. She says she grew up three streets from here. She says a lot of things.
Thank you, Jack, but they are not my size. And they are not for me, they are for the car.
Uwe, wiping his hands and looking at his Trabant the way other men look at a new baby.
Uwe, the mechanic of the courtyard, head and shoulders inside the Trabant, swearing at it in Saxon.
Welcome to the workers' paradise, Jack. Mind the ice, it has been here since 1983.
Ilse. Thank you for the telegram. Nobody else will speak to me. Every British embassy in Europe is waiting to arrest me.
Which is why you came to the one place in Europe with no British embassy. You are learning.

Listen. Every payment between Vasko and London went through East Berlin. The Stasi watched every one, and the Stasi file everything. Somewhere in the archive at Normannenstraße there is a file on Control's deal.
Proof. Proof that he's the traitor, not me.
Uwe will drive us. It is the only car in the building. Well, it is a car.
Scheibenkleister! The fan belt! Gone! Twelve years I waited for this car, and now I wait fifteen years for a fan belt!
Into the car, Jack. And bring your goose. The Stasi archive does not allow geese, so she will wait with me.
Don't look at my legs, Jack. These are the only Western tights in Prenzlauer Berg, and they are staying on.
Try the club downstairs. The singer wears nothing but holes. Some of them are held together with tights.
Normannenstraße. The Ministry for State Security. Ninety thousand people who do nothing but watch the other sixteen million. And one filing cabinet with Control's name in it.
Hear her? Like a sewing machine full of gravel. Beautiful. Get in, get in.
You want to go somewhere? Everybody wants to go somewhere. This car wants to go somewhere. But the fan belt is broken, and in the whole Republic there is not one fan belt until 1994.
Can't you use something else?
In the West, they say, you can use a lady's nylon stocking. In the West, ladies have nylon stockings. Here, a lady with nylons would sooner give you a kidney.
A stocking, a belt, a bootlace, anything that goes round and round. And not your scarf, I tried a scarf in 1981. It went round and round and then it went up in smoke.
Uwe. Would these do?
Fishnets! From Nina! Ha! She wore these when she sang at the Party youth festival. They had to stop the festival.
Round the crankshaft... round the dynamo... tie a knot...
She lives! Listen to her! Rrrrang-ang-ang-ang!
For you, Englishman. From my aunt in Hamburg. Real Western coffee. Keep it for an emergency. In this country everything is an emergency.
And when we get there, Jack? You walk up to the Stasi and ask nicely? You need a way in. Nina's father works there, I think.
Hey! Who let the Wessi in?
I'm not from the West. I'm from London.
Worse.
The Colonel has found the pogo. The Colonel is pogoing.
"Keine Zukunft": no future. In East Berlin that counts as optimism.
A stage made of pallets, two amplifiers built from radio parts, and a drum kit with nobody behind it. The sign says DRUMMER WANTED. OURS IS IN PRISON.
A portrait of the General Secretary, hung facing the wall. It's the most dangerous thing in the room, and they know it.
Nina: pink mohawk, leather jacket held together with safety pins, fishnet tights, and the voice of a very angry kettle.
Kalle the barman, writing in his notebook so fast the pencil is smoking.
Kalle the barman. He has a hearing aid with an aerial on it and a notebook he calls his "beer orders". Nobody orders that much beer.
God Save the Queen. With a goose. Very interesting. I mean, very nice. What was your name again? For the... beer orders.
Beer? We have one kind of beer. It is called beer.
Just a water, thanks.
Water. The Englishman drinks water. I will make a note. For the beer orders.
Go on, Englishman. Take Papa's pass, fix Uwe's car, and don't get caught. And come back and play the drums. The goose can sing.
What do you want, London? A photograph? We only pose for the Stasi, and they never send us copies.
I need your tights.
Excuse me?
For a Trabant. It's a long story.

It is always a long story with a Trabant. OK, London. Our drummer is in prison for his haircut, and I have no voice left. You get up there and sing something the Stasi will hate, and the tights are yours.
God save the Queen! The fascist regime!
Ha! The British anthem AND an insult to the State! Kalle is writing so fast his pencil is on fire!
Ninety-nine red balloons, go by...
A West German hit! In our cellar! They will close us for a month! Beautiful!
Risen from the ruins, and facing the future!
The national anthem, as a punk song! That is not even illegal, they just have no idea what to do! Look at Kalle, his face!
OK, London. You earned them. Take the tights. I have forty pairs. My mother works in a tights factory. It is the only thing the Five Year Plan ever got right.
And one more thing, since you are so interested in the Stasi. My Papa, Horst, is a night cleaner at Normannenstraße. He has flu. Take his coat and his pass.
Papa says the only person in the Stasi that nobody watches is the cleaner.
Filing cabinets, all the way into the dark. A hundred kilometres of files, they say: who you met, what you said, what you ate, and whether you enjoyed it.
There are more files here than there are people in Birmingham. I need to know where to look first.
"Wachsamkeit ist unsere Waffe." Vigilance is our weapon. Frau Kessler's weapon is a pair of knitting needles.
The Minister, watching the watchers. His eyes follow you round the room. They've probably been fitted with microphones too.
The Kartei: an index card for every file in the building. Tiny drawers, hundreds of them, each one labelled in Frau Kessler's perfect handwriting.
Hands off my Kartei, Horst! Cleaners clean. They do not read.
Keys on hooks, every one with a cardboard tag. One says SCHRANK 7.
Horst! Keys are not for cleaners! Cleaners have mops!
Schrank 7. Only with permission. Permission granted.
Cabinet 7, open, one folder lighter.
A steel cabinet with a big brass padlock. Number 7.
Locked, with a padlock the size of a fist.
The kitchen. I can hear a kettle, and Frau Kessler singing to it.
The staff kitchen, according to the sign. The only room in the building without a filing cabinet.
Frau Kessler is in there with her coffee. I'm not disturbing that.
That's Frau Kessler's kitchen. I'm a cleaner, not a suicide.
Frau Kessler, head archivist of the night shift: cardigan, spectacles, and a scarf she has been knitting since the building went up. She sees everything.
Mop, Horst. The corridor will not clean itself. Although in this building, I would not be surprised if it reported itself.
Yes, yes, Horst Brandt, I have seen it. Twenty-two years I have seen it.
Horst? You are late, Horst. Horst, you are taller.
Horst has flu, Frau Kessler. I'm his nephew. Jochen. From Leipzig.
Leipzig! Then you know my sister Gisela.
Of course! Lovely Gisela.
Lovely? Gisela? Hmm. You must be very polite in Leipzig.
Leipzig is a very big city.
Not so big. Everybody in Leipzig knows Gisela. Gisela makes sure of it.
Gisela... with the goats?
Ha! Yes! The goats! So you do know her. Poor boy.
Now: the mop, the bucket, the corridor. And do not touch my Kartei. Nobody touches my Kartei.
Frau Kessler. A present from my uncle. For the night shift.
Is that... Western coffee? Real coffee? Not Kaffee-Mix, with the peas in it?
I have not smelled real coffee since 1961. Horst, you are a good man. Your nephew is a good man. Everybody from Leipzig is a good man.
I make one pot. Just one. It takes twenty minutes. You mop. Mop!
Twenty minutes, and a building full of secrets. Start with the card index.
"HARROW, J. British agent. Weakness: takes his coffee black. Weakness: accompanied by a goose." Two weaknesses. They were thorough.
"GANS, WEISS. A white goose, answers to Colonel. Politically unreliable. Has bitten two officers of the Border Troops." Good girl.
"LONDON, British contact in the Vasko affair: see TEEKANNE." Teekanne. The Teapot.
"TEEKANNE: the Teapot. British contact, Vasko affair. Stirs his tea very loudly. Operative file in Schrank 7."
Even the Stasi noticed the tea.
I have what I came for. Time to leave, before Frau Kessler finishes her coffee.
Cabinet 7 holds a thousand files. I need a name first.
TEEKANNE. Photographs of Control with Vasko. Bank transfers from Zurich. And Control's own signature, on every page. That's him.
The Stasi put an alarm on their own filing cabinet. Of course they did.
Horst! That is not the mop! That is Schrank 7! You are not Horst, you are not the nephew, you are not even from Leipzig!
I am sorry about the coffee, Frau Kessler. Enjoy it anyway.
Wache! Guards! Guards! Also, thank you for the coffee! Guards!
The Wall from the western side: every inch painted, sprayed and signed. From the East it's grey. From the West it's the biggest noticeboard in the world.
A currywurst stand, closed. Currywurst: a sausage, cut up, drowned in ketchup and curry powder. Berlin's great gift to civilisation.
A black Mercedes with diplomatic plates. Franz always did like a nice car. On a barman's wages.
Ilse, covered in sand from head to foot and still somehow elegant.
Show him the file, Jack. And keep one hand on your wallet. Last time I saw Franz, he was pointing a gun at me.
Franz: barman, chef, London's man in Vienna, and now apparently chauffeur. He looks as if he hasn't slept either.
You have something for me, Herr Harrow? London sent me to fetch you home. Show me what you have, and we will see what London thinks of it.
Guten Morgen, Herr Harrow. Fräulein. And the Colonel. You are all very sandy.
Franz? How did you know where we'd come up?
There is only one tunnel under Bernauer Strasse that still works, and only one lady in Berlin who knows where it is.
Hello, Franz. You look older.
I am older, Fräulein. You look armed.
I am.
Operative file TEEKANNE. From the Stasi archive. Control and Vasko, together, with signatures. It proves he sold Nightglass. It proves it wasn't me.
Hm. Hm. Hmmm.
It is a fake, Herr Harrow.
What?
Look at this photograph. Control and Vasko in Moscow, March 1985. In March 1985 Control was in hospital having his appendix out. I sent him grapes.
And the paper. Western paper, from a London stationer. The Stasi never had paper this good. Somebody in London typed this file, and put it in Cabinet 7, where a clever man would find it.
Control wanted you to steal it.
Of course. A traitor, running into the West with forged Stasi papers. It is very convincing, Herr Harrow. For the prosecution.
Also, your goose is eating it.
Well. At least somebody enjoyed it.
Uwe has his head in the Trabant. Ask him what's wrong.
A stocking would do for a fan belt. Ilse won't part with hers. The singer in the club downstairs, perhaps.
Give the tights to Uwe, or put them on the Trabant myself.
I need a way into the archive. Nina said something about her father.
The Trabant is running. Get in.
Nothing to do here yet. Uwe needs help upstairs.
Nina's fishnets. She'll want something for them. Ask her.
Back up the steps to the Trabant.
Frau Kessler never takes her eyes off the Kartei. Something to take her mind off it: Uwe's coffee.
The card index will tell me which file, and where.
Cabinet 7 is locked. The keys are on the board by the desk.
Cabinet 7. Now.
Show Franz the file.
Nothing special.
That won't work.
I don't think so.
Not a chance.
That doesn't help here.
Those two don't go together.
Slowly, Jack. Those dogs can hear a mouse breathe.
What about a goose?
Nobody has ever tried it.
Nearly there. Smell that? Currywurst. The West.

A hundred and forty-five metres of sand, on elbows and knees, with a goose. At the far end a ladder, a cellar full of flour sacks, and a baker who says "Morgen" as if people climb out of his floor every day.
In Venice, the London buyer took off his mask: Control, Madame Novak's son. At dawn a telex went to every British embassy in Europe. Jack Harrow: traitor. Detain on sight.
Every road West is watched. So Jack goes where no British agent would ever go, and no British embassy can reach him: East Berlin. Ilse sent a telegram. It said only: "Come. Bring the goose."
Prenzlauer Berg: coal smoke, grey snow, and a courtyard where a man is shouting at a Trabant.
In an office above Whitehall a telex arrives: HARROW CROSSED TO WEST BERLIN 06:10. CARRYING STASI FILE, AS EXPECTED. Control reads it twice, and stirs his tea. Loudly.
Fake.
Chapter Eight: All In.
Nina's fishnet tights, more hole than tights. In the West they would be fashion. In the East they are a political statement. In a Trabant they are a fan belt.
Horst Brandt, night cleaner, Ministry for State Security, Normannenstraße. The photograph could be anybody in a flat cap. Tonight it's me.
A vacuum pack of real Western coffee from Uwe's aunt in Hamburg. In East Berlin this is worth more than the Trabant. Possibly more than Uwe.
A brass key with a cardboard tag: SCHRANK 7. NUR MIT GENEHMIGUNG. Only with permission. I'm giving myself permission.
Operative file TEEKANNE, the Teapot: a British contact who arranged every payment between Colonel Vasko and London. Photographs, bank transfers, and a signature I know very well.
The Trabant does sixty downhill, forty on the flat, and fills Frankfurter Allee with blue smoke. Nobody looks twice. Every car in East Berlin fills Frankfurter Allee with blue smoke.

The Ministry for State Security: a whole city block of grey windows, lit all night. At the side door a guard looks at a pass, at a flat cap, at a mop and bucket, and yawns. Horst Brandt, night cleaner, reporting for work.
Down the back stairs with a mop in one hand and a Stasi file in the other. Out through the bins. Into a Trabant with its engine running, a goose in the back and Ilse at the wheel.

A bakery on the wrong side of the Wall, with a tunnel under the floor that has not been used since 1964. Ilse knows it. Ilse knows everything. "Crawl when the dog walks," she says. "Freeze when the dog listens."
